title: $H-T$ Phase diagram of CeRh$_{2}$As$_{2}$: Refinement of the parity-switch scenario
authors: Changhee Lee, P. M. R. Brydon
abstract: The superconductivity of CeRh$_2$As$_2$ has drawn attention due to its first-order transition in magnetic fields. At first glance, the multiple superconducting (SC) phases as well as the first-order transition appear consistent with the parity-switch scenario, which emphasizes the role of strong Rashba spin-orbit coupling enabled by the locally non-centrosymmetric crystal structure. However, experimental phase diagrams exhibit notable deviations from this simple picture: thermodynamic measurements reveal a nearly vertical phase boundary of the high-field SC phase despite the orbital depairing effect, while transport measurements show that the initial slope of the high-field SC phase is steeper than that of the low-field SC phase. Here, we show that these discrepancies can be understood by considering the combined effects of nonsymmorphic band structure and coexisting antiferromagnetic order. We demonstrate that the symmetry-enforced electronic structure around the Dirac node and type-II Van Hove saddle points near the X point in the Brillouin zone boundary becomes more anisotropic with increased interlayer hopping amplitude, and this anisotropic band structure naturally accounts for the anomalous initial slope of the odd-parity SC phase. Meanwhile, a phenomenological theory incorporating coexisting antiferromagnetism explains the nearly vertical thermodynamic phase boundary as a consequence of field-enhanced odd-parity superconductivity enabled by the over-suppression of Pauli depairing.
summary: This paper refines the understanding of superconductivity in CeRh2As2 by addressing conflicts between transport and thermodynamic measurements. The authors propose that anisotropic band structures near specific points in the Brillouin zone explain slope discrepancies, while coupling SC order with coexisting antiferromagnetism accounts for unusual phase boundaries.
main_problem: The study aims to reconcile experimental discrepancies in the H-T phase diagram of CeRh2As2, particularly concerning the superconducting (SC) state's dependence on magnetic fields and temperature.
main_result: Anisotropic band structure near the X point explains the anomalous initial slope of the odd-parity SC phase, while coexisting antiferromagnetism provides a mechanism for the nearly vertical thermodynamic phase boundary.
method: The work combines theoretical modeling using k.p Hamiltonians and Landau free energy formalisms with analysis of experimental transport and thermodynamic measurements.
model_or_system: The system is the heavy fermion superconductor CeRh2As2, modeled by considering nonsymmorphic band structure features (Dirac nodes, Van Hove singularities) and incorporating coexisting antiferromagnetic order parameters into a Landau theory framework.
key_observables: H-T phase boundaries for SC phases (even/odd parity), initial slopes of the superconducting transition lines in transport measurements, and thermodynamic signatures like specific heat anomalies.
important_parameters: Interlayer hopping amplitude ($t_{\perp}$), anisotropy ratio ($\alpha$), magnetic field strength (H), and temperature (T).
main_assumptions: The standard Ginzburg-Landau theory is insufficient due to anisotropic band structure; the analysis relies on incorporating coexisting AFM order into a phenomenological Landau free energy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic H-T phase diagrams comparing transport and thermodynamic measurements, and show Fermi surfaces highlighting Van Hove singularities near the X point in the Brillouin zone boundary.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies experimental discrepancies between SC phases. It then uses k.p modeling to explain the anisotropic band structure causing slope anomalies. Finally, it employs a phenomenological Landau theory incorporating AFM order to account for the vertical thermodynamic phase boundary.
why_interesting: Although focused on heavy fermions, the detailed analysis of symmetry-enforced electronic structure (nonsymmorphic symmetries) and pairing mechanisms in strongly correlated materials provides advanced insights into how crystal structure dictates quantum ground states, relevant to understanding complex many-body Hamiltonians.
